paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Davis, Oklahoma, took place in August 1910, when white townsmen threatened the town's Black population after a Black man struck a white man with a brickbat. A local report said about 25 of some 75 Black residents fled, most to Ardmore, while an Oklahoma City dispatch said every Black resident was driven out.

Davis had a Black population of about 75 in 1910, according to the Daily Ardmoreite. On Thursday, August 18, a Black man named Asbury Milton was ordered out of the Freeman store and, when he refused to go, was forcibly ejected by R. Y. Steadman, a white man. Milton then struck Steadman with a brickbat, inflicting what the Ardmoreite called a serious head wound.

Angered by the assault, some of the town's "toughs" made threats against the Black residents. About 25 left that night, most for Ardmore, and a few others were expected to follow. An Oklahoma City dispatch went further: "every negro was driven from the town" on Friday night and Saturday morning, August 19 and 20.

On August 19 the town's business men assured the remaining Black residents of their safety, and no further trouble was expected. Neither report mentions an arrest, either of Milton or of the men who made the threats.

The episode appears in the coverage only in two Oklahoma white papers. The Daily Ardmoreite, published where most of the refugees went, ran a front-page Davis report on August 19 headed "Race Trouble at Davis Yesterday," calling the men who made threats "toughs." The Tulsa Daily World's short Oklahoma City item of August 21, "Negroes Run Out of Davis," called Steadman "a leading citizen" and explained the expulsion by white anger at the assault. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The local Ardmoreite account, written the day after the fight, described a partial flight on August 18, while the later Oklahoma City dispatch described a complete expulsion on August 19 and 20. They also spell the assailant's name differently, as Asbury Milton in the Ardmoreite and Melton Asberry in the Tulsa paper.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Davis, Oklahoma
bases: Both reports describe Black residents leaving Davis under white threats after a fight, A1 as a partial flight of about 25 people and A2 as every Black resident 'driven from the town'.

A1 (local Davis dispatch) and A2 (separate Oklahoma City dispatch with different name spellings and timing) agree that Black residents left Davis under white anger after a Black man struck R. Y. Steadman, though they differ on how many left and when.

accounts.label: Local Davis dispatch
accounts.gist: Town 'toughs' threatened the Black residents after the assault; about 25 left that night, a few more were expected to go, and business men assured the rest of their safety.

accounts.label: Oklahoma City wire
accounts.gist: Enraged whites drove every Black resident from Davis on Friday night and Saturday morning.

framing.detail: The Ardmoreite's 'Race Trouble at Davis' presented the assault as fact and called the men who threatened Black residents 'toughs', while noting business men's assurances of safety.
The Tulsa World's 'Negroes Run Out of Davis' reported the expulsion flatly and explained it by the assault on 'a leading citizen'.

info: The fight at the store took place on Thursday, Aug. 18, 1910 ('yesterday' in an Aug. 19 dispatch); about 25 Black residents left that night.
Davis, Oklahoma; most who fled went to Ardmore.
The Black residents of Davis, a population of about 75; about 25 left the first night (A1), or every Black resident (A2).

A Black man, Asbury Milton (A1) or Melton Asberry (A2), was reported to have struck R. Y. Steadman, a white man, with a brickbat after Steadman ordered him out of the Freeman store and forcibly ejected him.
Some of the town's 'toughs' (A1); 'the whites' who 'became enraged' (A2).

quotes: Incensed at the negro's action, some of the town's "toughs" made threats against the blacks, which resulted in about 25 of the negroes leaving last night, most of them going to Ardmore.
the business men of the town today assured the negroes of their safety and no further trouble is expected.
